Chicago will double its efforts to assist people experiencing mental health crises, expanding its citywide response program beginning next week.

Starting Monday, the Crisis Assistance Response and Engagement (CARE) program will extend its hours of operation to 8 a.m. to 10 p.m. Monday through Friday and add a second shift of evening staff.

“This program ensures that we no longer criminalize and traumatize individuals in crisis, but instead we offer them pathways to heal,” Mayor Brandon Johnson said at a news conference Friday at the Lawndale Mental Health Center on the Near West Side.

In May, Johnson announced the city would use $5.2 million from the final round of federal pandemic relief funding allocated to Chicago to launch an expansion of the program. Beyond that initial investment, the mayor said he was counting on revenue from his controversial social media tax to sustain and further expand the program.

CARE, run by the Chicago Department of Public Health, deploys one mental health clinician and one emergency medical technician to respond to eligible 911 calls involving mental health crises and socio-emotional distress.

The program is now fully staffed for citywide operations, with eight teams deployed across Chicago and two alternate teams to handle non-emergency CARE responses.

Ald. Rossana Rodriguez Sanchez (33rd) speaks at the Lawndale Mental Health Center in Chicago Friday during a news conference announcing the expansion of the Community Assistance and Recovery Engagement (CARE) program’s hours of operation.

Octavio Jones/For the Sun-Times

“This latest expansion will alleviate the burden of calls that police and firefighters receive for mental health crises and social emotional distress, enabling them to focus on their core duties of protecting our communities while mental health professionals focus on mental health,” Johnson said.

CARE teams respond to requests for mental health services made through 911 dispatch or the program’s non-emergency email. City officials said 911 dispatchers may also initiate a CARE team response without a request if a call is deemed eligible.

Eligible situations include non-violent, non-medical crises where there is no active threat to the individual or others, according to city officials.

CARE teams will also have greater access to information through the city’s new computer-aided dispatch system.

Although CARE teams have always had access to police and fire radio communications, those channels provide limited information. Previously, teams could primarily see the address associated with a call, without access to additional details that could help them better assess the situation before responding.
